idiom_name: fixed-timestep driver loop with a lag accumulator and interpolated rendering
implementation_notes: Language-neutral shape: one loop owns the cadence. It reads a monotonic clock, converts real elapsed time into simulation time with a lag accumulator, advances the simulation in fixed dt steps until the accumulator falls below dt, clamps the accumulated lag (and caps steps per frame) so a slow frame cannot trigger runaway catch-up, drains input without blocking, and renders the current (possibly interpolated) state. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - the loop, the clock read and the pacing sleep are written over the platform's timing primitives, and the pattern is the discipline that keeps input, update and render separate inside one loop. Two invariants do the work: measure elapsed time from a monotonic source instead of trusting a requested sleep or timer period, and pass simulation time as an explicit dt into the update instead of letting the simulation read the clock.
code_sketch:
prev = monotonic_now(); dt = 1/60; lag = 0
while running:
    now = monotonic_now(); lag += now - prev; prev = now
    lag = min(lag, MAX_LAG)              # no spiral of death
    input.drain()                        # never block
    while lag >= dt: world.step(dt); lag -= dt
    render(alpha = lag / dt)             # interpolate previous -> current
    idle_until(next_deadline)            # yield/sleep, then re-measure
pitfalls: Real elapsed time comes from timers that overshoot and can be interrupted; if the loop trusts the requested sleep or timer period instead of re-reading the clock, the simulation drifts.
Without a clamp on accumulated lag and a cap on steps per frame, a slow frame triggers more catch-up work, which makes the next frame later - the spiral of death.
Feeding raw frame deltas into physics is the classic failure: behaviour depends on frame rate, becomes non-deterministic and can go unstable where damping was tuned.
Measuring intervals with a wall clock (system time, epoch-based timers) makes the simulation jump when the clock is adjusted; use a monotonic source.

Wrong move: treat requestAnimationFrame as a fixed simulation tick -> refresh rates and background throttling change callback cadence -> instead use its timestamp to feed a capped fixed-step accumulator and pause or clamp simulation time when visibility changes.

Wrong move: assume Unity FixedUpdate runs exactly once per rendered frame -> low frame rates can run multiple fixed updates and high frame rates can run none -> instead keep physics in the fixed phase and interpolation or presentation in the frame phase.

Wrong move: put physics and transforms in Godot _process -> the variable render cadence makes behavior frame-rate-dependent and can fight interpolation -> instead advance gameplay physics in _physics_process and reserve _process for presentation.

Arcadeon Studios (2026), 'Turn Your Game Loop into a Testable System — Fixed-Step Determinism' - input-frame design, serialisable SimState, ring-buffer recorder and deterministic replay implementation. https://arcadeonstudios.co.uk/blog/turn-your-game-loop-into-a-testable-system-fixed-step-determinism
